1.Nf3 e6 2.c4.name: English Opening: Agincourt Defence
1.Nf3 e6 2.c4.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 e6 2.Nf3, one of White's two usual replies to 1...e6 in the English Opening. Black intends a supported ...d5, comparable to the French Defence, and the game often transposes to other lines, most commonly the Queen's Gambit Declined or the Catalan Opening.
1.Nf3 e6 2.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 before Black has occupied it, while the d-pawn waits so that the game can still become a queen's pawn game, a set-up with the king's bishop on the long diagonal or a flank opening. The cost is that no pawn stands in the centre yet: Black can build there, and White has to show that the pressure is worth it.

1.Nf3 e6 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, giving White space and a clear plan at once. The cost is commitment: Black can challenge the pawn at once or take a solid stand in the centre. A classical queen's pawn game with a direct fight for the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 and short castling; the bishop will bear on the long diagonal once the knight has moved. White keeps the centre flexible but leaves it to Black, who can take space in the centre. A slower, manoeuvring game in which White's pressure builds up gradually.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack
1.Nf3 e6 2.b3.background: The opening is often reached by transposition, particularly with 1.Nf3 followed by 2.b3, as here. Aron Nimzowitsch experimented with 1.b3 in the 1920s and 1930s but more commonly used the order 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3; Bent Larsen played 1.b3 frequently between 1968 and 1972.
1.Nf3 e6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which aims along the long diagonal at e5 and f6 and controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. White stays flexible and solid, but Black is free to build a pawn centre, so the game is about whether White can undermine it later.

1.Nf3 e6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and steers towards a French Defence, since Black's pawn is already on e6. The move is sound, but Black decides the game's character, from a solid pawn chain to an early strike at White's centre with the c-pawn.

1.Nf3 e6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares d4 in a solid set-up. It is modest: once d4 follows, the e3-pawn shuts in the c1-bishop, and since nothing contests d5, Black builds a centre comfortably.

1.Nf3 e6 2.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop and prepares e4, usually in a set-up built around a fianchettoed king's bishop. The structure is solid but modest: Black takes space in the centre, and White's play depends on achieving e4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal for the queen, but it develops nothing and takes c3 from the queen's knight. Black takes space in the centre unchallenged, and a later c4 would cost White another tempo.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and watches d5 and e4, but it blocks the c-pawn, so set-ups with c4 are off for now. Black can take the centre at once or attack the knight with 2...Bb4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.a3.strategy: A waiting move that prepares b4 but does nothing for the centre or for development. White spends a tempo on the wing while Black takes space with ...d5 and develops freely.

1.Nf3 e6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops ...b5, but it costs a tempo and does not help White in the centre. Black takes space in the centre and develops without being challenged.

1.Nf3 e6 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from a black knight, but the c8-bishop is shut in behind e6 and no piece is ready to land on g4, so the tempo is wasted. Black takes the centre while White still has to develop.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Na3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes c4 and b5 but does nothing for the centre. After 2...Bxa3 3.bxa3 White has the bishop pair and the b-file, yet the doubled, isolated a-pawns are a lasting weakness, and 2...d5 simply takes the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Ne5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to a square where 2...d6 attacks it, and it must retreat; after 3.Nc4 even 3...d5 gains another tempo. White has lost time while Black builds a pawn centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Nd4.strategy: Centralises the knight, but 2...c5 or 2...e5 attacks it at once and it must move again, for example back to f3 or to the rim at b3 or b5. Black gains central space with tempo.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Ng1.strategy: Retreats the knight to its starting square and undoes the first move. White has lost two tempi, and Black, with ...e6 already played, is effectively a move ahead.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b4.strategy: Gambits the b-pawn without enough in return: the f8-bishop, freed by ...e6, takes it with 2...Bxb4 and nothing recaptures. Attacking the bishop afterwards only gains a few tempi, since it can simply retreat.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space, but nothing defends the g4-pawn, and the king's pawn cover is loosened for good. Black can attack the pawn at once with 2...h5 or simply take the centre, and the advance has done nothing for White's development.

1.Nf3 e6 2.h4.strategy: A wing-pawn push that develops nothing and gives Black time to take the centre. It weakens g4, and the idea of Ng5 is easily met by ...h6.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Rg1.strategy: The rook can step to g1 only because the knight has left; the move forfeits castling kingside for good and develops nothing. Black takes the centre with ...d5 while White's king stays in the middle.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Ng5.strategy: Loses the knight: the pawn move ...e6 has opened the diagonal from d8, so 2...Qxg5 takes it, and nothing guards g5 because the c1-bishop is blocked by the d2-pawn.

1.Nf3 e6 2.Nh4.strategy: Loses the knight to 2...Qxh4, since ...e6 has opened the d8-h4 diagonal and nothing guards h4. White gets nothing in return.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its most natural square, where it controls e4 and d5 and commits nothing in the centre. Black can still choose between a solid pawn centre and a Queen's-Indian-style fianchetto. The price is that White may complete the bishop-and-pawn set-up on its own terms without being disturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and, with the e6-pawn behind it, makes e4 hard for White to achieve. The solid pawn pair costs a little: the c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 until a fianchetto gives it the long diagonal. From that sound base Black can fight for d4 and e5.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 c5.strategy: Contests d4 from the flank and keeps the choice between a pawn on d5 and a fianchetto open. Black reaches a flexible structure that can turn into a symmetrical English-style one if White plays c4. White can build quietly or fight for the centre, so neither side is forced into a fixed plan.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 f5.strategy: Takes e4 under control and heads for a Dutch set-up, with a Stonewall chain as one way to build it. The pawn loosens the e8–h5 diagonal, and once Black has a pawn on d5, e5 becomes a hole that White's bishop and a knight can use. The move is committal: Black fights for the initiative at the cost of some kingside safety.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes d4 and e5, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so …c5 is ruled out for now. Once Bb2 is played, …e5 would leave the pawn attacked twice and defended only once, so Black must prepare it first. Sound, though less flexible than developing the king's knight or striking at the centre at once.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and, once the king's knight is out, clears the way for castling, keeping …d5 and …c5 for later. After 3.Bb2 the g7-pawn is attacked and no longer guarded by the bishop, so Black has to block the diagonal at once. Sound, but less direct than developing the knight or striking at the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the d2-pawn, so d3 and d4 are impossible until White drives the bishop away or blocks the diagonal. After 3.Bb2 the g7-pawn is attacked and no longer guarded by the bishop, so Black has to block the diagonal. Playable, but the bishop has no clear target and may have to move again.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 b6.strategy: Prepares …Bb7 to oppose Bb2 on the long diagonal. The structure is solid but somewhat passive, since Black mostly reacts to White's plan and has little quick counterplay.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 c6.strategy: Prepares …d5 with a Semi-Slav-style chain of pawns on c6, d5 and e6. The move is slow, takes c6 from the b8-knight and leaves the c8-bishop shut in once …d5 is played, so White gets time to develop and take the centre. Sound, though …d5 at once is more direct.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 d6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn pair on d6 and e6 that keeps e5 under control against the coming Bb2. It concedes central space, and the c8-bishop has only d7 to go to until …b6 follows, so White develops and takes the centre at leisure. Sound, though passive.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 g6.strategy: Prepares …Bg7 against the coming Bb2, but after 3.Bb2 the h8-rook is attacked along the long diagonal and …Bg7 loses the bishop to Bxg7, so Black first has to block the diagonal. With pawns on e6 and g6, the dark squares f6 and h6 also grow weak once the dark-squared bishops are exchanged. Sound, but clumsier than natural development.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but controls neither d4 nor e5. Once e3 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal, Bxa6 bxa6 would double Black's a-pawns, and White develops undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Qe7.strategy: Puts the queen in front of the f8-bishop and blocks its only open diagonal, so Black's kingside development waits. 3.Ba3 attacks the queen along the a3–f8 diagonal at once, and Black has to block or move the queen again.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Qf6.strategy: Attacks the undefended a1-rook along the open long diagonal and rules out Bb2 for the moment, because Qxb2 would win the bishop. Once White blocks the diagonal the threat is parried, and the queen is exposed to Ne4 and to the pawn advance e4–e5 while Black's development lags.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d7-pawn, so …d5 is impossible while the bishop stays on d6, and the bishop becomes a target for a later e4–e5. White develops freely and takes space in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop where 3.d4 attacks it, so White gains central space with tempo while the bishop has to move again.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, aiming at f5 and g4 but doing nothing for the centre. Once the d-pawn moves, Bxh6 gxh6 would double Black's h-pawns, and White develops and takes the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop, whose natural square is e7, and passes up …Nf6, the knight's best square. The bishop stays shut in until the knight moves again or …g6 follows, and White develops freely and takes space in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre; it prepares …b5 at best. White takes the lead in development.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 a5.strategy: Prepares …a4 against the b3-pawn, but spends a tempo on the flank while the centre is uncontested. White develops undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 b5.strategy: Advances a flank pawn without developing a piece, and nothing guards it on b5. Once the e-pawn moves, the f1-bishop attacks it, and Black must spend another tempo on …a6 or …c6 to hold it.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, which is left with e7 and h6, and opens the e8–h5 diagonal towards the king without developing a piece. White simply develops and claims the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 h6.strategy: Rules out Ng5 and a later Bg5 in advance, but neither is a threat, so the move only costs a tempo while the centre stays uncontested. White develops and takes the centre undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook pawn without a purpose: it develops nothing, leaves the centre to White and loosens the kingside, where …h6 is no longer available to drive a piece from g5. White develops at leisure.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Qg5.strategy: Hangs the queen at once: the f3-knight attacks g5, and Nxg5 wins it for nothing.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Qh4.strategy: Hangs the queen at once: the f3-knight attacks h4, and Nxh4 wins it for nothing.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's d8–h4 diagonal. 3.Ba3+ checks at once along the open a3–f8 diagonal, and Black must answer with …d6, which is then pinned, or another king move, since …c5 loses a pawn to Bxc5+.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: nothing defends a3, and Bxa3 or Nxa3 wins it for nothing.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside and opens the long diagonal to the h8-rook. 3.Bb2 attacks the rook, and every answer costs something: …Bg7 drops the bishop to Bxg7, …Nf6 cuts the queen off from g5 so Nxg5 wins a pawn, and …f6 leaves the kingside full of holes.

1.Nf3 e6 2.b3 e5.strategy: Spends a second move on the e-pawn and hangs it: the f3-knight attacks e5 and nothing defends it, so Nxe5 wins a pawn.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: The flexible choice: Black develops a piece and commits the pawns to nothing, so a Queen's Gambit, Catalan, Indian or symmetrical set-up all stay possible. The price is that White decides which structure arises, and Black has to be at home in several.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre at once and heads for a Queen's Gambit type of position, with the e6-pawn solidly supporting d5. The price is the c8-bishop, shut in behind the pawn chain until Black finds a way to free it.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Takes control of d4 and heads for a symmetrical English structure, with the pawn already on e6 so that ...d5 stays available. The price is that a later ...d5 can leave Black with an isolated d-pawn or hanging pawns.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and eyes d4 and e5, but it blocks the c-pawn, so ...c5 is ruled out for now. White can take the centre at once. Sound, though less flexible than developing the other knight or striking in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Be7.strategy: Develops the dark-squared bishop and clears the way for castling, keeping ...d5 for later. It gives up the active ...Bb4 and leaves White free to shape the centre. Sound, but slower and less flexible than developing the knight or striking in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop with a pin on the d2-pawn, so d4 is impossible until White blocks the diagonal or drives the bishop away. Playable, but the bishop has no clear target as long as White does not play d4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 on the long diagonal, to press on the centre from a distance. White can claim central space at once, so Black must be ready to hit the centre later. Sound and flexible, but a less direct fight for the centre than a central pawn move or developing the knight.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid pawn structure. The move is slow and takes c6 from the b8-knight, and White can answer with a fianchetto instead. Sound, but less flexible than developing or striking in the centre at once.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn pair on d6 and e6, behind which Black develops and later aims to break in the centre. It does not contest e4, so White is free to build a broad centre. Playable and solid, though passive.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 f5.strategy: Heads for a Dutch-type set-up and takes e4 under control. It loosens the e8–h5 diagonal and, in a Stonewall structure, leaves a hole on e5. Sound enough, but committal and less solid than ...d5.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which presses along the long diagonal. It does nothing for the centre at once, so White can build there first. A flexible but slow set-up; a direct fight for the centre is better.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Places the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but leaves d5 and the centre uncontested. White takes space while Black has lost time.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Qe7.strategy: Brings the queen out early to e7, where it blocks the f8-bishop's only open diagonal, so the kingside pieces are slow to develop. White builds the centre and gains time.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the g8-knight. The attack on b2 is empty, since ...Qxb2 loses the queen to Bxb2, and White gains time by driving the queen back.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d7-pawn, so ...d5 is impossible while the bishop stays on d6, and the bishop is a target for White's knight and central pawns. White simply builds the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop where d4 attacks it, so White gains central space with a tempo while the bishop has to move again.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim. After d4 the c1-bishop attacks it, and Bxh6 gxh6 would double the h-pawns, while ...Nf5 can be met by e4 with a gain of time.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop and passes up the natural ...Nf6. The knight supports ...d5 from e7, but the bishop stays shut in until the knight moves again or Black fianchettoes it, and White gains time in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that neither fights for the centre nor develops a piece; it prepares ...b5 at best, which c4 already restrains. White simply carries on developing undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Advances the a-pawn without purpose, weakening b5 and the queenside for a tempo. White builds the centre undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, which is left with e7 and h6, and opens the e8–h5 diagonal towards the king, with no development in return. White builds a broad centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside for good and does nothing for the centre or development. The queen guards g5, but d4 adds the c1-bishop as a second attacker, so Black must spend another tempo on ...h6 or ...g4, and after ...g4 Ne5 the pawn becomes a target.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Rules out Bg5 and Ng5 in advance, but neither is a threat yet, so the move mainly costs a tempo while the centre is still uncontested. White builds the centre undisturbed.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook pawn without purpose and loses a tempo; ...h6 is no longer available to drive a bishop or knight from g5. White simply builds the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Qg5.strategy: Places the queen on a square attacked by the f3-knight; Nxg5 wins it outright.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Qh4.strategy: The f3-knight attacks h4 and nothing defends the queen, so Nxh4 wins it at once.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's diagonal, with nothing gained. The king stays in the centre, where it becomes a target once White opens the position with d4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 Ba3.strategy: Gives the bishop away: bxa3 or Nxa3 takes it, and Black gets nothing in return.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: cxb5 takes it, and Black has no real compensation for it.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Spends a second move on the e-pawn and loses it: nothing defends e5, so Nxe5 wins a pawn, and Black has no development to show for it.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it controls b5, d5 and e4. Black's ...a6 hints at a queenside advance, and with the c4 pawn the knight makes that advance harder to carry out.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and opens the c1-bishop and the queen. Black's ...a6 was a slow move, so White uses the time to claim space; the d4 pawn will be challenged, and White commits to a game of central tension.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: the bishop on g2 will work along the long diagonal and White can castle quickly. A flexible, low-risk set-up that keeps the central pawn break for later, at the price of letting Black claim the centre first.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and the d4 square, and builds the a6 and c5 structure that supports a later challenge to the c4 pawn. Black has not yet decided how to set up in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, the very idea behind 1...e6. The e6 pawn holds d5 firmly; the price is a light-squared bishop shut in behind the pawns. Black accepts a slightly passive but sound game, and ...a6 costs a move without doing harm.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 and d5 before committing the pawns. Black keeps every central set-up open and prepares quick castling; the cost is that White gets to decide the pawn structure first.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto so the bishop on g2 will aim at b7 and the queenside, exactly where Black's pawns are heading, once the f3 knight steps aside. White develops solidly and keeps the centre flexible.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.d4.strategy: Challenges the c5 pawn at once. If Black takes, the recapture Nxd4 gives White a central knight, the c4 pawn controlling d5 and more space, against a compact but passive structure on a6 and e6. White commits to open play with a lead in space.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.b3.strategy: Prepares to develop the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, a quiet set-up that aims at the centre from a distance. Sound but slow: it spends a move on a flank pawn and lets Black take the centre first.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.g3 b5.name: Zukertort Opening: Shabalov Gambit
1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.g3 b5.strategy: A pawn sacrifice to open the a- and b-files and seize the initiative on the queenside. White takes the pawn and ends a pawn up, and Black's compensation is activity rather than anything concrete.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight where it watches e4 and d5, so White's central pawn advances meet resistance. Black keeps the flexible set-up of pawns on a6, c5 and e6 and decides later how to meet the fianchetto.

1.Nf3 e6 2.c4 a6 3.Nc3 c5 4.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight against d4, so White cannot build a pawn centre there without support. Black commits the knight early, but kingside development and castling stay open.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and, with ...e6 already played, builds the solid French-style pair of pawns on d5 and e6. Black gets a firm hold on the centre and a closed, manoeuvring game against White's flexible set-up. The price is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight, which controls d5 and e4. Black keeps the choice between a solid pawn on d5 and a fianchetto of the queen's bishop, but no pawn stands in the centre yet, so White can still set up as it likes.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 and keeps the knights and the d-pawn flexible. If White opens the centre, Black has the c-pawn against White's d-pawn with ...e6 already played; if not, it is a slower game on the queenside and the long diagonal. Black has not developed a piece yet.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5 and keeps a central pawn move and the other knight's development available. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c5 is ruled out for now. Sound, but the knight is committed before the pawn structure is settled.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling in a solid set-up. It makes no claim on the centre, so White is free to choose its own plan. Sound, but less direct than a central pawn move or developing the knight.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which gives the c8-bishop an open diagonal and contests the long diagonal against White's coming bishop on g2. No black pawn claims the centre yet. Sound, but slower than claiming the centre or developing the knight.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...Bb7 against the long diagonal. Nothing guards the b5-pawn, so a4 attacks it at once. The move does nothing for the centre, where a pawn on d5 is the more direct claim.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a compact chain of pawns on c6, d5 and e6, and takes b5 and d5 under control. Once ...d5 is in, the c8-bishop is shut in behind e6. Sound, but slower than playing ...d5 immediately.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares a compact set-up, perhaps with a later central pawn break. It concedes central space, since White can take the centre at once without a black pawn to challenge it. Sound, though passive.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and heads for a set-up built around the f5-pawn, developing the kingside pieces and then closing the centre with the d-pawn. The pawn weakens the e8-h5 diagonal, and once the d-pawn stands on d5 the e5-square becomes a hole for a white knight.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and a mirrored fianchetto, with short castling to follow. No black pawn claims the centre yet, so White can take space freely. Sound, though slow.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the edge, where it eyes b4 and c5 but has little influence on the centre. White gains time to take the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Qe7.strategy: Puts the queen in front of the f8-bishop and blocks its only open diagonal, so Black's kingside development waits until the queen moves again. White simply develops and takes the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it eyes b2, which the c1-bishop guards, and takes f6 from the g8-knight. After 3.d4 the bishop can come to g5 and attack the queen with tempo.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d-pawn, so ...d5 is impossible until the bishop moves again, and leaves the bishop a target for a later e4-e5. White develops and takes the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Bc5.strategy: Eyes f2, which the king guards, but 3.d4 attacks the bishop, which must move again while White has taken the centre with tempo.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Bb4.strategy: Looks at d2, which is guarded several times, so there is no threat, and 3.c3 drives the bishop away with a useful move that also prepares d4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Aims for f5, but the knight stands on the rim in the meantime, and once the d-pawn has moved, Bxh6 gxh6 leaves Black with doubled h-pawns. White can later drive the knight from f5 with g4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop, whose natural square is e7, and stakes no claim in the centre. Black's kingside development lags while White takes space.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 but spends a tempo without developing a piece or claiming central space.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 a5.strategy: Controls b4 but takes no part in the centre and weakens b5, which the a-pawn can no longer cover.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight and loosens the e6-pawn and the e8-h5 diagonal without developing a piece. White can aim at the weakened light squares.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Prepares ...g4 against the f3-knight, but loosens the kingside for good. Only the queen guards the pawn, so once the d-pawn has moved, the c1-bishop joins the knight against it and Black must spend more time on its defence.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 h6.strategy: A prophylactic pawn move that spends a tempo with nothing concrete to prevent, develops no piece and claims no central space.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 against g3, but spends a tempo on a flank advance that weakens g5 and the kingside and develops nothing. White can stop the idea for good with h4.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's d8-h4 diagonal. After d4 the c1-bishop can come to g5 with check, while the king stays stuck in the centre.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Qg5.strategy: Puts the queen on a square attacked by the f3-knight, which takes it with 3.Nxg5 because no Black piece defends g5.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Qh4.strategy: Walks the queen into the attack of both the f3-knight and the g3-pawn, so 3.Nxh4 or 3.gxh4 wins it for nothing.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 Ba3.strategy: The b2-pawn and the b1-knight both attack a3, so 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 wins the bishop outright.

1.Nf3 e6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: the f3-knight attacks e5 and nothing defends it, so 3.Nxe5 wins it. After 3...Qg5, 4.d4 uncovers the c1-bishop against the queen and keeps the knight protected.
